topic: Defining & Recognizing Sepsis — Sepsis-3, SOFA, qSOFA & Screening
speakerAffiliation: Virtual Teaching Hospital · Acute Medical Unit
speakerBio: An acute physician who runs the hospital's sepsis screening programme and has audited every missed case for a decade. His mantra: score the organs, not the inflammation.
lectureHTML:
🎯 Where we start

It is 3 a.m. A 72-year-old man on the surgical ward has a respiratory rate of 24, a systolic of 98, and keeps drifting off mid-sentence. The night registrar glances at the chart: "He's not septic — his white count is normal and he's not spiking a temperature." That sentence, built entirely on the old SIRS mindset, is about to cost hours. This session is about never making that mistake — recognising sepsis by organ dysfunction, not by inflammation.

1 · The one sentence that holds the whole topic

Sepsis is suspected infection + new organ dysfunction. Septic shock is sepsis that still needs vasopressors and is still making lactate after you have filled the tank.

Everything in this session is an operational way of detecting those two states early and reproducibly.

2 · Why we abandoned SIRS 🪦

For two decades sepsis meant "SIRS + infection." The Systemic Inflammatory Response Syndrome criteria were: temperature <36 or >38 °C, heart rate >90, respiratory rate >20 (or PaCO₂ <4.3 kPa), and white cells <4 or >12 ×10⁹/L. Two of four made you SIRS-positive. The problem became obvious:

  • Too sensitive and non-specific: anyone who runs up a flight of stairs, or has a hangover, or is in pain meets 2/4. SIRS is just "the body is stressed."
  • It missed sick patients: a landmark study (Kaukonen, NEJM 2015) found that 1 in 8 patients with infection and organ failure who died were SIRS-negative. The criteria that were supposed to catch sepsis let the dying slip through.
  • It measured inflammation, not danger. SIRS tells you the host is responding; it says nothing about whether an organ is failing — which, as Session 1 established, is what actually defines sepsis.
⚔️ Contrast pair — SIRS vs Sepsis-3

SIRS (1991/2001): infection + ≥2 inflammation criteria. Detects inflammation. Over-calls the well, under-calls the dying. Sepsis-3 (2016): infection + organ dysfunction (rise in SOFA ≥2). Detects danger. The whole reform was a shift from "is the body inflamed?" to "is an organ failing?"

3 · Sepsis-3 — the definitions you must quote 📖

The Third International Consensus (Singer et al., JAMA 2016) — "Sepsis-3" — gives us two, and only two, clinical entities:

TermDefinitionOperational criteria
SepsisLife-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infectionSuspected/confirmed infection + an acute rise in SOFA score ≥ 2 points from baseline
Septic shockA subset of sepsis with circulatory and cellular/metabolic abnormalities profound enough to substantially increase mortalitySepsis + vasopressors needed to keep MAP ≥ 65 mmHg AND lactate > 2 mmol/L, both persisting despite adequate fluid resuscitation

Note what vanished: the term "severe sepsis" is obsolete under Sepsis-3. Sepsis is the severe entity now — if there's no organ dysfunction, it's just infection.

💡 One-liner — the septic shock triad

Septic shock = vasopressors + MAP <65 without them + lactate >2, all after fluids. Get this exactly: it is AND, not OR. Hypotension needing pressors and a raised lactate and despite fluid. This subgroup carries a hospital mortality > 40%, roughly double that of sepsis without shock.

4 · SOFA — measuring organ dysfunction 🧮

The Sequential (formerly Sepsis-related) Organ Failure Assessment scores six organ systems from 0 (normal) to 4 (worst), giving 0–24 total. A rise of ≥2 points attributable to infection defines sepsis. You are not expected to compute it from memory at the bedside for screening — but you must know the six domains:

SystemVariableWorsening marker
🫁 RespirationPaO₂/FiO₂ ratioFalling ratio (<40 kPa / <300; severe <13.3 kPa / <100 with support)
🩸 CoagulationPlateletsFalling count (<150 → <20 ×10⁹/L)
🫀 LiverBilirubinRising bilirubin (>20 → >204 µmol/L)
💉 CardiovascularMAP / vasopressor doseMAP <70; then escalating noradrenaline/dopamine requirement
🧠 CNSGlasgow Coma ScaleFalling GCS (15 → <6)
🫘 RenalCreatinine / urine outputRising creatinine (>110 µmol/L) or oliguria (<500 → <200 mL/day)

Assume a baseline SOFA of 0 in patients not known to have pre-existing organ dysfunction. The elegance is that it captures the multi-organ nature of the disease drawn out in Session 1 — respiration, coagulation, and cardiovascular collapse are exactly the endothelial and immunothrombotic failures we traced.

5 · qSOFA — the bedside trigger, and its limits ⚡

SOFA needs bloods and a blood gas. For rapid bedside identification outside critical care, Sepsis-3 offered quick SOFA (qSOFA) — three purely clinical items, no labs:

qSOFA criterionThreshold
Respiratory rate≥ 22 /min
Systolic blood pressure≤ 100 mmHg
Altered mentationGCS < 15 (any new confusion)

Two or more of three (a "positive qSOFA") flags a patient with infection who is at high risk of a poor outcome and should trigger escalation, closer monitoring, and a full septic work-up.

⚠️ Danger — qSOFA is a prognostic flag, NOT a rule-out

The 2021 Surviving Sepsis Campaign explicitly recommends against using qSOFA as a single screening tool. Its sensitivity is poor — a patient can be dying of sepsis with a qSOFA of 0 or 1. It was validated to predict mortality, not to catch early sepsis. Use it to raise alarm when positive, but never to reassure yourself when negative. A qSOFA of 1 in a patient your gut says is sick is still a septic patient until proven otherwise.

6 · NEWS2 — the screening tool the wards actually run 📋

Because qSOFA under-detects, most health systems screen with an aggregate early-warning score. In the UK that is NEWS2 (National Early Warning Score 2), which sums seven physiological parameters:

  • Respiratory rate, SpO₂ (with a separate scale for hypercapnic/COPD patients), supplemental oxygen, temperature, systolic BP, heart rate, and level of consciousness (ACVPU — including new confusion).
  • A NEWS2 ≥ 5, or a score of 3 in any single parameter, is the trigger threshold that should prompt urgent review and active consideration of sepsis.
  • Its strength over qSOFA is sensitivity: it flags deterioration earlier, before hypotension is established. Its cost is lower specificity — it over-calls, which for a screen is the safer error.
💡 Pearl — screen wide, define narrow

Use a sensitive tool (NEWS2) to screen and a specific framework (Sepsis-3 / SOFA) to define. The screen's job is to never miss; the definition's job is to be right. Confusing the two — using qSOFA to screen, or SIRS to define — is how patients fall through the net.

7 · The recognition workflow at the bedside 🔁

  1. Suspect infection? Source symptoms, fever/hypothermia, or simply an unexplained deterioration.
  2. Screen for danger with your local tool (NEWS2 ≥5, or qSOFA ≥2). Any positive → escalate.
  3. Look for organ dysfunction — new confusion, RR ≥22, SBP ≤100, oliguria, mottling, a lactate, falling platelets, rising creatinine/bilirubin. A SOFA rise ≥2 confirms sepsis.
  4. Give fluids, then reassess. Still needing pressors for MAP ≥65 and lactate >2? That is septic shock — the highest-acuity label.
  5. Start the Hour-1 bundle (Session 3) the moment you suspect sepsis — do not wait for the SOFA arithmetic.

8 · Lactate — the number that ties it all together 📈

Lactate appears in both the definition of septic shock and the resuscitation bundle, so understand what it means. A raised lactate (>2 mmol/L, and especially ≥4) in sepsis reflects tissue hypoperfusion and the cytopathic hypoxia of Session 1 — anaerobic metabolism because cells cannot get or use oxygen. It is a marker of severity and a resuscitation target: failure of lactate to clear with treatment predicts death. Beware confounders (adrenaline infusions, liver failure, metformin, salbutamol) — but in an infected, deteriorating patient, treat a high lactate as hypoperfusion until proven otherwise.

☠️ M&M — "Normal white count, sent back to the ward"

A 79-year-old woman with a perforated diverticulum was reviewed at 2 a.m. Temperature 36.4, WBC 9.1 — so by the old SIRS reflex she "didn't look septic" and the escalation call was stood down. But her RR was 26, her SBP was 96, and she was newly muddled: a qSOFA of 3 and a NEWS2 of 7. She arrested from septic shock four hours later; her admission lactate, run belatedly, had been 5.1. Lesson: a normal temperature and white count do not exclude sepsis — that is precisely the SIRS trap Sepsis-3 was built to close. Elderly and immunosuppressed patients are often afebrile and normo-leucocytic. Score the organs, not the inflammation.

9 · Take-home wiring diagram

  • SIRS is dead as a definition — too non-specific, and it missed 1 in 8 dying patients.
  • Sepsis-3: sepsis = infection + SOFA rise ≥2 (organ dysfunction). "Severe sepsis" is obsolete.
  • Septic shock: vasopressors for MAP ≥65 AND lactate >2, both despite fluids — mortality >40%.
  • qSOFA (RR ≥22, SBP ≤100, altered mentation) — a prognostic flag, not a screen; never rule out sepsis on a negative qSOFA.
  • NEWS2 ≥5 is the sensitive ward screen; screen wide, define narrow.
  • Lactate is both a severity marker and a resuscitation target.

Next session: the clock starts. Once you've recognised sepsis, what must happen in the first sixty minutes — the Surviving Sepsis Campaign Hour-1 bundle.

moderatorQs.q: Walk us through the precise difference between sepsis and septic shock under Sepsis-3, and why the distinction changes the numbers at the bedside.
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Sepsis is suspected infection plus an acute rise in SOFA of ≥2 points — i.e. new organ dysfunction. Septic shock is a subset: after adequate fluid resuscitation the patient still needs vasopressors to maintain a MAP ≥65 mmHg and has a lactate >2 mmol/L. Both conditions must be met, and both must persist despite fluids — it is an AND, not an OR. The distinction matters because septic shock identifies a circulatory-and-metabolic failure subgroup with hospital mortality above 40%, roughly double that of sepsis without shock. Labelling shock correctly escalates the patient to vasopressor-capable care and mandates the full bundle without delay.

moderatorQs.q: The Surviving Sepsis Campaign recommends against qSOFA as a single screening tool. If qSOFA is part of Sepsis-3, why the caution?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Because qSOFA was derived and validated to predict mortality in patients with suspected infection, not to detect early sepsis. Its specificity is reasonable but its sensitivity is poor — a substantial number of genuinely septic patients score 0 or 1, particularly before hypotension develops. As a screen, a tool that misses cases is dangerous, so SSC 2021 advises against relying on it alone and favours more sensitive aggregate scores such as NEWS2. The correct use is asymmetric: a positive qSOFA (≥2 of RR ≥22, SBP ≤100, altered mentation) is a strong prompt to escalate, but a negative qSOFA must never be used to reassure or rule sepsis out.

moderatorQs.q: Why did Sepsis-3 move away from SIRS, and what concrete evidence supported the change?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: SIRS measures inflammation, not organ dysfunction — and inflammation is neither specific to infection (exercise, pain, trauma trigger it) nor synonymous with danger. It over-diagnosed the well and, critically, under-diagnosed the dying: Kaukonen et al. (NEJM 2015) showed that around 1 in 8 ICU patients with infection and organ failure who died were SIRS-negative, meaning a SIRS-based definition would have failed to flag them. Sepsis-3 therefore re-anchored the definition on organ dysfunction (a SOFA rise ≥2), matching the pathophysiology — sepsis is defined by the host response damaging organs, not merely by the presence of inflammation. 'Severe sepsis' was retired because, under the new framework, sepsis is by definition already the organ-dysfunction state.

audienceQs.q: My patient has an infection and a lactate of 2.5 but a normal blood pressure and no pressors. Is that septic shock?
audienceQs.answerHTML: No. Septic shock requires both a vasopressor requirement to keep MAP ≥65 and a lactate >2, and both must persist after adequate fluids. Your patient has a raised lactate but no vasopressor need, so this is sepsis with hypoperfusion, not septic shock — still a serious, bundle-triggering diagnosis. The right move is to treat it as sepsis: give the fluids, start the Hour-1 bundle, and remeasure the lactate. If after resuscitation they become hypotensive enough to need vasopressors while the lactate stays >2, the label — and the acuity — escalates to septic shock.

audienceQs.q: We screen with NEWS2, but the doctors talk about qSOFA and SOFA. How do these fit together on the ward?
audienceQs.answerHTML: They do different jobs. NEWS2 is your screening tool — deliberately sensitive, run on every patient, and a score ≥5 (or 3 in any single parameter) should trigger urgent medical review and a sepsis thought. qSOFA (RR ≥22, SBP ≤100, new confusion) is a quick bedside risk flag — if 2 or 3 are present the patient is high-risk and needs escalation, but a low qSOFA does not clear them. SOFA is the fuller, labs-based score doctors use to confirm organ dysfunction and define sepsis (a rise ≥2). In short: NEWS2 to catch, qSOFA to flag, SOFA to define. Your escalation on a NEWS2 ≥5 is exactly the right trigger.

audienceQs.q: Why is lactate such a big deal — isn't it just from muscles working hard?
audienceQs.answerHTML: In sepsis, a raised lactate mainly reflects tissue hypoperfusion and cellular oxygen failure — anaerobic metabolism because cells can't get or use oxygen (the cytopathic hypoxia from Session 1), not just exertion. That's why it appears in the definition of septic shock (>2 mmol/L) and as a resuscitation target in the bundle (remeasure if >2; ≥4 is high-risk). Failure of lactate to fall with treatment predicts a worse outcome. There are confounders — adrenaline infusions, liver failure, metformin, salbutamol can all raise it — but in an infected, deteriorating patient you treat a high lactate as hypoperfusion until proven otherwise.
